doc.title: Reggie Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

title: Chala Nata and Maynard's love of India
summary: Rowe asks about the tune Chala Nata from Watkins's record One for Miles One for Maynard; Maynard visited an ashram in India, and the piece is by Jay Chattaway.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Great. Let’s talk about composing. I’ll try to do this, a name this tune [scats] that was very bad. [piano] Right, but that’s not what I meant to say.
This is one of your things.
This is one of my things. Give it to me again.
[scats] Then when it comes down it’s minor. It’s on your website and it’s called “Chala Nata”

Oh “Chala Nata.” So that’s not my composition. But that is from my second record called “One for Miles One for Maynard” — two of my biggest influences. Miles, purely as a listener I was influenced and he was an idol of mine, and of course Maynard being my boss and somebody influencing me on a daily basis. Maynard loved to talk about India. And Maynard during a certain period of his life, his seventies, sixties I think it started. And a lot of people don’t know this about Maynard. You know Maynard lived with Timothy Leary. Did you know that? And his entire family.

But he would go to India once a year for several months to an Ashram of a guy named Sai Baba. They called him Sri Sathya Sai Baba and he was a spiritual leader. Maynard loved Sai Baba. He would go there, you know as he would say, once a year for six weeks or two months where it would be a cultural exchange. He would teach music, jazz, and then he would learn Indian music. He loved Indian music. So “Chala Nata” was a product of him wanting to have something in the repertoire — and that’s not the only thing, there were other tunes like that that were Indian-flavored, Indian jazz fusion stuff [piano].
That’s what I was trying to sing.
So that was my tribute to Maynard Ferguson. I knew how much he loved Indian music and I love that chart.
Yeah. I like the way it starts out like sort of ethereal.
It’s absolutely — the jazz part of it or the American take on it is very seventies popular music.
Right. And then even when the drum thing starts it’s very boo-ga-loo-ish.
[Scats] that kind of like Ringo Starr almost. Yeah. So I wanted to do an updated version of that. But it’s not my composition. The composer of that is Jay Chattaway.
